utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have two matters to deal with before we proceed at all with the evidence today. The first is a question I want to direct to Mr. Hannis. The Chamber is faced with an application for certification of a decision made about the evidence of General Clark, and it's an anxious and difficult decision for us to reach, particularly bearing in mind the need to satisfy the second leg of the test. So I don't hide from you the fact that it's not easy for us to decide it. Coincidentally, however, we've received a further submission in relation to the evidence of the witnesses -- the other two American witnesses who are not yet resolved. And in one of the footnotes to that submission it is said: "The Trial Chamber made clear in its second decision on the Prosecution motion for leave to amend its 65 ter list to add Wesley Clark that the Defence must be able to cross-examine on matters related to credibility of a witness. The United States Government now expressly narrows its requested protective measures for all USG Rule 70 witnesses to allow the Defence to question on these matters." Now, that on the face of it indicates that it's acceptable in relation to all these witnesses. And what we would like is clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try and obtain that clarification for you. My last communication with the US indicated that was their position with regard to Burns and Philips however it appears it may still be a lingering issue regarding General Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I -- you can understand that being at the stage we're at that the -- any significant change in circumstances may be a matter far better dealt with by the Trial Chamber than at a later stage in the proceedings, and that's why it would be helpful to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I've conveyed that and the US is aware of our timetable as well with end of evidence for -- projected for the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if that's possible to do that today, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because of the time difference we aren't able to hear from Washington until late in the day. I will do what I can, Your Honour, because it is a matter that has been the subject of ongoing discussions. I think when I raised it last, no action was being taken because of our pending request for certification, and it seemed to be that they were waiting the outcome of that to make what I guess is a tougher decision for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it is a -- one has to, I think, immediately comment that it's a difficult distinction to understand, so that's why -- we read it the way it was meant to be but then thought perhaps it should be clarified, because it was a submission in relation to a different matter. So we shall leave that matter in your hands and hope that you can relay an answer to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll do so at the earliest possible moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now turn to deal with the various objections that were taken to the edited report of Philip Coo which was intimated to the parties and tendered to the Court as his proposed Rule 92 ter statement. I first of all want to make it clear that the Trial Chamber rejects the Defence submission that the proximity of the witness to the Prosecution team is a bar to him giving evidence of fact. There's nothing wrong, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, with an investigator giving evidence of fact. It is also our view that the fact that he was present at interviews of accused and witnesses does not bar him from giving evidence, either. Indeed, he might even be the vehicle through which evidence is tendered to the Court of what was said by an accused person in an interview and indeed by a witness where there's an issue over the credibility of the witness. We also reject the notion that no part of this report could ever be presented to the Court as his statement; however, in its present form it is entirely unacceptable. So in other words, we do reject it in its present form as an unsuitable way of presenting his evidence. It is essentially the same report as was originally prepared by him as an expert witness, and even in this redacted form it is riddled with expressions of opinion that would be appropriate for only an expert to express. It is also riddled with expressions of conclusions that are for the Court and not for a witness of fact to draw. He interprets material where it's for the Court to interpret it, he speculates in some instances that events in one year must have been such and such because of the circumstances of another year, he reaches conclusions based on limited identified source material, he provides analysis in certain circumstances. And broadly speaking, the Trial Chamber has accepted the criticisms -- the detailed criticisms of the content of this report that were advanced by the Defence. That having been said, if Mr. Coo, as investigator, has obtained information, particularly in the form of documents, and he is on the face of it the appropriate vehicle through which to introduce factual information, including documentary material, then there is no objection to that being done. However, we do note that the documents that are referred to in the report fall into a number of categories which on the face of it don't appear to be matters he ought to be dealing with at all. For example, there are 140 documents that are laws, decrees, rules, orders, decisions, or plans that should be capable of presentation to the Court in a written submission. And hopefully, many of them are the subject of agreement, if not already admitted. There are 31 Serbian print media reports, and these are matters in general which the Chamber has said it will exclude unless satisfied, particularly satisfied, about the authenticity of what is said in a press report. And we gave examples before of reporting particularly by press -- by radio and television, but also by print media of the precise terms of an interview. They also include, I think, 17 television or radio programmes and references to 12 web sites. Some of these web site references are obviously relevant and admissible, but in relation to others, there must be some doubt and therefore, again, it may be that the best way of dealing with this is through a written filing. Where we see the limit of Mr. Coo as a vehicle for presentation of material is that he can tell us what was recovered, he can tell us how on the face of material documents recovered they might relate to each other, he might even tell us how documents could possibly have a bearing on events; but for him to tell us that they do or that they appear to him to have some bearing on the events that supports or corroborates other evidence is quite wrong, in view of the earlier decision we took. What we would encourage you to do is -- as a Prosecution team is to follow earlier guidance we've given about written submissions covering authenticity, reliability, relevance, and probative value. Orders and decisions were made in relation to earlier applications to admit documents as free-standing documents, and these orders and decisions contain guidance on how to satisfy the Trial Chamber about the admissibility of these. We also at that stage invited you to specify how the documents tendered fitted into the case, and again you've clearly tried to do it through Mr. Coo going too far, as it were, but it can be done either by him or by you in a written filing within acceptable limits. I can't tell -- we can't tell whether Mr. Coo remains an essential witness in the light of this, but we do not mean for one moment to suggest he's not a person who should give evidence here. It's a question of tailoring what's presented to satisfy, first of all, the original decision made; secondly, the various orders about presentation of evidence that have been made; and lastly, the restrictions that apply to a witness of fact. Now, we understood that parties were anxious for an early determination of this. Obviously, it was a major exercise for the Trial Chamber, and this is as quickly as it could be done. That's why this decision has been given orally rather than in writing, because preparing carefully crafted written decision does take a lot of time. I hope that's comprehensive enough, but we are prepared to offer further guidance should parties seek it in relation to particular elements of what has been decided. We hope to be helpful and not to impede the introduction of any evidence that is going to assist us to arrive at a just conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thank you for that guidance, Your Honour. We will take note of your remarks this morning and work on how we proceed with Mr. Coo. I would inform the Court that we had anticipated filing today a written submission concerning a number of exhibits along the previous guidance you have given us and as we are done for some witnesses like General Vasiljevic and General DZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, there was one other thing I meant to say to you, that I think it is in relation to Vasiljevic that -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just checking which witness this order relates to, but you may find, if you refer yourself to your own -- to the decision of the 15th of February on the admission of exhibits, and it is in the case of - and it is in relation to Vasiljevic - a good example of you achieving the standards we had set and that you might find following that is the way to proceed. If, Mr. Hannis, you already have in mind a filing, I think it would be unwise to hold it back to add to it. It would be helpful if you've got something ready to tender it as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. We do intend to file that today, Your Honour, and then I anticipate we perhaps will be doing another one related to documents regarding Mr. Coo that we don't have on this current list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If there's nothing further, Your Honour, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That exhausts the matters that I wish to deal with, but I was told that Mr. Lukic might have procedural issues, also -- or Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. I believe Mr. Fila has the first word on this, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we bring in the next witness, I wish to raise an issue as follows: Yesterday at 2115, less than 12 hours before the start of the session, I received additional information about Witness Protic from Mr. Stamp, if I'm correct, and at around 11.00 I received this in the Serbian language. Probably the Prosecutor thinks I ought to sit by my screen all night so that I can receive information whenever it suits them. On page 3 of this information - because you know there are manners and politeness to be observed - there are additional comments and suddenly a sentence turned up that the witness was aware that Nikola Sainovic was responsible from Kosovo from 1989, I wish to stress this, for some 20 years. Yesterday I heard from Witness Crosland that he was collecting electricity bills on Kosovo and now we will hear -- excuse me -- yesterday we heard from Witness Kickert that Sainovic collected electricity bills from OIDP down there and now I hear from another witness that he did this for 20 years. I think that according to Rule 65 ter, there's no mention of Sainovic in the documents. I read all the witness statements, including this Protic, but Rule 65 ter on the 10th of May, 2006, has no mention of Sainovic. According to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt just briefly. Mr. Stamp, is 1989 correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is supplementary information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Secondly, are you leading evidence about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers the question. If it's information given to you about what the witness can say, but the Prosecution do not intend to lead that evidence; therefore, there's no need for them to amend the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the witness is not to be examined on Sainovic, then I don't need to say this. But if he is examined about Sainovic, I have to object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's not going to be, you've been told, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am then very happy that last night at 9.00 p.m. I received unnecessary information which made me nervous all night. Thank you. Pay them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our concerns also relate to this material that was received last night and to material that was received I believe March the 6th was the original disclosure of a transcript, a fairly lengthy transcript, from some proceedings in Belgrade relating to this witness. The main problem that we have is that we have been quite anxious for this witness for quite some time to get information from the Office of the Prosecutor since the information disclosed for him was rather scant [Realtime transcript read in error "constant"]. Toward that end, earlier this week I had sent some e-mail inquiries to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding any statements they have of the witness -- relating to whether they have any additional witnesses for the witness and in particular an OTP statement for the witness and whether he has been questioned, et cetera, so we can get information and details. The response at that time was no we have nothing. Line 18 of the transcript of this page says "rather constant." I said "rather scant," so that should be corrected. But in any event, we now -- first of all, the testimony that was tendered to us two days ago for the first time gives details that would appear to contradict items that had been disclosed for him previously, but we were not in a position, obviously, to go out into the field and verify some of these matters. In particular he mentions the names of several other individuals, including a General Obrad Stevanovic, who seemed to all of a sudden fit the description of individuals who have previously been identified as Sreten Lukic in the prior statements of the witness. And now where the 65 ter summary for this witness was very, very general and stated that -- left one with the impression that he did not know specific dates for anything. Now all of a sudden in the three pages of supplemental information sheet that we received last night, it's replete with quite specific details that had we had earlier we could have undertaken some efforts to seek out documentation or verification or contradiction for which we could try to confront the witness. The most glaring example I can give you is that in the previous discussions that the -- the previous statements and interviews that were given to us, Mr. Protic claimed that his communications were via mobile phone and did not make any reference to anything else. Now in the supplemental information sheet he gives very specific fixed locations, official phones that he used that, if we had had this knowledge prior to last night, we would have at least tried to have obtained documentation to verify whether, in fact, the phone calls were made from such official land-lines, as he now claims. I really don't know how to -- I don't know what to ask for for relief, Your Honour, so I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we may have reached a witness then where it may be necessary for you at a later stage to invite the Court to re-call him, or it may be that you take advantage of your inability in one sense to confront him and invite us to treat his evidence less -- as less reliable -- or less weighty, I suppose, in light of later evidence you submit in the Defence case, because obviously you still have loads of time to carry out your inquiries and present other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, I agree. I am just very frustrated at this stage that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it also has to be said that there has been great difficulty in securing the attendance of this witness, and therefore it's understandable that there may be matters coming to light now. We've been very critical of the Prosecution in general for not interviewing witnesses at an earlier stage, but there's a limit to how easy it might be to do that, and this is one where they plainly have had difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They -- it's my understanding he gave public testimony in Belgrade a month ago and that the OTP did have a representative at those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's public, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore, that applies to both. I assume that you're taking cognizance of these developments, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to as much as we can. So I just want to bring that to Your Honours' attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's a very fair way to present this, but we will briefly discuss it and decide whether we think there's anything else that ought be done at this stage. Before doing that, I will hear if Mr. Stamp wants to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just two matters. We disclosed everything we have had from this witness at the earliest available opportunity, firstly; and without sort of doing an inventory of every factual submission by my learned friend just now, which I would not agree with as being entirely correct, I just say that if there are these contradictions, as he has suggested, then there are -- there would be, if they existed, pretty obvious on the face of the documents that he has been given and matters worthy of cross-examination if that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We note the observations that have been made. We will proceed to hear the evidence of this witness. If a remedy is required, we shall deal with that at the stage when the matter is presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That witness, Your Honours, is Bozidar Protic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Protic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Please make yourself comfortable, Mr. Protic. And I can't see what you've taken from your bag at the moment, but if it is documents please don't refer to them at this stage. Any documents -- oh, it's just simply your glasses. Okay. Thank you. Our system here, which may be different from any other system you've experience of, involves immediate questioning by counsel rather than the Judges. And we start with the Prosecutor, who will ask you questions, and then you will be cross-examined by those counsel for the accused who wish to do so. It may be that there is only one of the Defence counsel who wishes to do so; it's not clear at the moment and it will depend on your evidence. We'll start straight away with the Prosecutor, and that is Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Protic. Could we start by you stating your full name.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Very well. Bozidar Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you still employed or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to retirement, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I worked for the Ministry of the Interior as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you a member of the police force of the -- the police force of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: From 1975 until the date of my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I understand that in respect to certain events that occurred during your employment as a driver with the Ministry of the Interior in 1999, you were interviewed by an investigative judge, one Mr. Dilparic, Milan Dilparic on the 5th of December, 2003. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that interview was recorded on tape and the tape was played over to you and you affirmed that it was correct. Do you recall that as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A couple years later on the 29th of June, 2006, do you recall giving a sworn statement to the prosecutor Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Objection. I don't remember that there is a sworn statement in front of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. My friend is probably correct, depending on how you use the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you gave the statement to Mr. Stankovic, you were cautioned about your obligation to speak the truth under Serbian law and the law in respect to perjury if you did not speak the truth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Correct. Judge Dilparic warned me that before the Court I should tell the truth and nothing but the truth, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But let's move now to the 29th of June, 2006. You said that that date you gave a statement to the Deputy War Crimes Prime Minister [sic] Dragoljub Stankovic. Do you recall that he cautioned you of your obligation to tell the truth on that occasion and not to withhold information and that false testimony constituted a criminal offence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, mistake, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here Prime Minister Dragoljub Stankovic. It was the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, yes, I note that, and no doubt, it will be corrected. It doesn't alter the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that, Mr. Protic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If my learned friend could point out in the statement given by -- to the Prosecutor where this witness was cautioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one I have, Mr. Lukic, at the bottom of the first page in the English: "Having been advised pursuant to Article 102, paragraph 2 of the ZKP to tell the truth and not withhold information. He was then warned that giving false testimony constitutes a criminal offence."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the 8th of February this year, that's last month, did you testify in respect to the same matters in a trial in Belgrade before the Belgrade District Court?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I testified there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review the record of these three different occasions when you spoke about these events in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes. After each of my testimonies, I was given records of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was what you said in -- on each of those three occasions true, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You did, however, indicate that there were a couple matters you wanted to correct, and I'd like to just take you through them briefly. In this statement you gave to Mr. Stankovic at pages 3 to 4 of the English version, and it's 2 to 3 of the B/C/S version, we see at the top of the English version here it is written: "I made three trips to the 13th May

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is stated in the record by Prosecutor Stankovic that when you spoke to Mr. Sreten Lukic, he addressed you by your first name. Is that correct? How did he address you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: By my family name, Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we refrain from the leading questions from now on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's possibly fortunate that the answer was not contained in the question on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe I lead in respect to what is already said in the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but this is a good example of where I think it's not a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It undoubtedly will devalue the evidence in this sort of situation. If you feel the need to ask questions orally of a witness who has already answered many questions in writing, I think they still need to be open questions; otherwise, their value will be lost. utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. There might be an issue with respect to security of a witness, and I'm wondering if perhaps we could go into private session briefly for me to raise it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Normally, the senior -- the superiors or supervisors would address their subordinates by their first name unless they were officially informing them of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What name did Mr. Lukic use to refer to you? What did he call you when he spoke with you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Normally he would address me by my last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at other times what would he call you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He always addressed me by my last name, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he have a particular way of addressing you when he addressed you by your last name? What word did he use, if you can recall, to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a passage we should be looking at in this connection, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is in the English transcript. This is the third-to-last paragraph and it is in the last three lines. He just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what page, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of -- page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The record of Mr. Stankovic reads: "I suppose that he recognised my voice, as he addressed me by my first name," and the witness says he addressed him as Protic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't seem to have that. This is page 2 of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 2 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said it was the last three lines of a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last three lines of the third-to-last paragraph of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. Thank you. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Because of the circumstances in which we managed to get this testimony or this witness here, we have sent the material as quickly as it was available. We sent originally the draft transcript to the CLSS to prepare official, final transcript as early as possible, and when we got that we sent them. I think that Your Honours should have the last final translations from CLSS. So if it is not you do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I've found it now. I just was looking in the wrong place. Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last correction we could make, Mr. Protic, if we then move on. It is recorded at page 7 of the English version of the transcript of your testimony in February that you stopped by at the station in -- the police station in Kladovo and spoke to chief Sperlic. Is that name correct, Sperlic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember the name of the chief of police in Kladovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes. His last name is Sperlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement or the transcript of the interview by the investigating judge dated the 5th of December, 2003, is marked P2816. The statement the witness made to the Prosecutor Stankovic of the 29th of June, 2006, is marked P2817. And his testimony before the district court in Belgrade is marked 2824, that testimony dated the 8th of February, 2007. I tender the three documents, subject to the correction that he has just made, and ask that they be received in evidence under Rule 89(F) in lieu of oral testimony he could give in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that we have already announced that we are going to object the admission of the testimony from this year that has been disclosed to us late, and we also think that, actually, none of these statements could be admitted under 92 ter rule. I would leave it to Your Honours to decide on that. Definitely we would object the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The motion is to admit them under 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because in the 65 ter statement of this witness it's under 92 ter, so it's -- created the confusion. But anyways we would object if it's proposed to be admitted under 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only suggested basis for opposing this is the late notification. That's an issue we've really dealt with already in the earlier decision made in relation to Mr. Ivetic's objection and therefore we will admit these three documents. I would just like to try to clarify one thing, and that is the reference on page 2 of the English. But what I would like on the screen is the third-last paragraph in English on page 2 in the B/C/S, and that's of P2816. Now, that's not the document I have got as 2816. Is the 5th of -- sorry. No. It is my mistake. Sorry. It's 2817. Mr. Protic, you'll see on the screen part of your statement which you gave to the Prosecutor Stankovic, and if you look at the large paragraph filling the middle of the page, the centre of the page mainly, and go to the end of that paragraph, could you read to me the last two sentences. The part where it says: "I suppose that he recognised my voice ..." Could you read that and the rest to the end of the paragraph, that's two sentences at the end. Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what it is that I'm supposed to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see the -- on your screen at the moment, the top paragraph that you can see on the screen, go to the end of that paragraph and read to me the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the first occasion he ordered me to go to Janjevo and to report," is that the part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. It's the part immediately before that, the end of the paragraph above that, the very end of it, the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the part where it says: "I presume" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I presume that he recognised my voice, too, because he addressed me by name. And on that occasion…

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Stop there. Read it again, the same sentence, read it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I presume that he recognised my voice, too, because he addressed me by name." It should in fact say "by my last name."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I wanted to check the accuracy of our English translation, and it would appear that we have an inaccurate English translation which is not a matter for you, but that's why we were trying to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you have exact translation. He made mistake. He said differently today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That, Mr. Lukic, is a matter for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the translation was not wrong and is not wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The witness has read the words in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the interpreter has interpreted them. Are you challenging that interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, but we have different in the statement and in the testimony today; that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I'm clarifying is what the witness said in his statement, and it's inaccurately translated in English as I understand it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in B/C/S "ime" is first name, "prezime" is last name, so it is not incorrectly translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- correct the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. What you're doing is challenging the translation, as I understand it. You're challenging what the interpreter has just told us the witness said. And if that's the case, I will have it reported upon by CLSS, as we have done in the past. But let's be clear what it is we are challenging. Now, you're challenging the way in which the interpreter today has translated the words of Mr. Protic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In line -- Your Honour, in line 23, page 23, line 18, it's correctly translated. "I presume" -- it just escaped. "I presumed that he recognised my voice, too, because he addressed me by name" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the -- that's fine, and that's what I understood the interpreter to say. But that's not what the English says. The English translation says: "By my first name," and that's the bit I was clarifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Name, first name is the same meaning in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the interpreter able to give any guidance on this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S term "ime" can indeed be interpreted both as first name and as name. The interpreter strived to take the neutral form.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Note of the French booth: In the Serbian version it is the word "first name" which is used and not just "name" or "surname." It is first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, it's back to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, whatever the translation is here, Mr. Protic, you recall what he would call you. What would he call you on formal occasions when you were among other police personnel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In the presence of others, by my last name officially as Protic. When we were on our own sometimes he would call me Protic and sometimes Proto.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, it is perhaps unclear from the three statements exactly where you went to and where you delivered bodies to on the four trips that you spoke of. So I'm just going to ask you quickly to take us through them one by one. On the first trip, where did you collect bodies from and where did you deliver them to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: On the first occasion I received orders from my immediate superior Dragic Nenadic, who told me that he had spoken to General Zekovic, and he told me that through my friends I should find a truck for me to carry out a task which was very important and which was in the interest of the state. I did that. I had a friend, Tode Kurbalija, a refugee from Croatia, who had a Mercedes truck with a temporary licence plate, 18BG and the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Protic. What you just told us is in two of the statements we have before us. I just simply want to clarify: From where did you pick up bodies on your first trip and where did you deliver them to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: A place called Tekija, not far from Kladovo, from a refrigerator truck which had appeared from the Danube. And the bodies were put from there onto the truck and I drove them to Batajnica. And that was the first trip I made of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many bodies were there? Just a number. Give me a figure. How many bodies were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Fifty-four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we pull up P600. This is an item which is already in evidence, Your Honours. I do apologise. It is not indicated on the notification, but it should not present much of a problem, I don't think. It is a photograph. Could you just blow it up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recognise this vehicle, Mr. Protic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a Mercedes truck. It's got a -- it's green and it has a white container on top and it said "Mesna Industrija," meat industry "Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, have you seen this truck before, the one depicted in this picture; and where, if you have?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it in the place called Tekija after it was dragged out of the Danube, and later on in pieces near Petrovo Selo where it was destroyed with explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did this truck contain -- when you saw it in Tekija first, did it contain anything? What were the contents of the truck when you saw it in Tekija first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you have the answer to that at line 15, on page 26, as complete an answer, I think, as you could expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I was hoping that he would refer to the particular truck and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you saw it destroyed -- or could I ask you to explain what you mean when you say that you saw it later in pieces near Petrovo Selo where it was destroyed in pieces. When was it that you saw it in pieces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I saw it in pieces when I brought the next load of bodies from the place called Janjevo. I passed by the truck, very close by it, before entering the centre. It was on a clearing on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did you come to know that it was destroyed by explosives?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I heard from the people who were working there, and also I recognised the truck because I was familiar with parts of it. I could recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said your second trip, just now, was from Janjevo to Petrovo Selo; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many bodies did you transport on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Seventeen or 19. I think it's more likely to be 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the third trip was -- where did you collect the bodies and where did you deliver them to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The southern part of Kosovska Mitrovica, near the freight railway station, in a wood industry shed where there were channels for fixing machinery and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where did you deliver them to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: To Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this a different area in Petrovo Selo as the previous trip or was it the same place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The same place near the centre, but not the same pit. It was another pit very close to the first one; less than 50 or 60 metres apart, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many bodies did you transport on that trip?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Fifty-five or 56. Over 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The fourth and final trip that you made, where did you collect the bodies and where did you deliver them to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: More or less in the centre of Pristina, near the publishing house or the newspaper house. It was called Rilindija. There was a refrigerator truck on the parking lot. It was the largest size that such trucks come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where did you take these bodies to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: To Batajnica, to the centre for special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, about how many bodies did you take on that fourth trip?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The refrigerator truck was closed. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: (redacted). I didn't see them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you told us that General Zekovic gave you the phone number --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need to know which statement because we have several.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to Mr. Stankovic and in -- in both the statements that you gave to Mr. Stankovic and the interview with Mr. Dilparic you said that you got the orders to go and collect the bodies from General Zekovic, and in both of those statements you also said that you were given a contact phone number to call when you were in Kosovo, on the three occasions that you went to Kosovo. On the first occasion you went to Kosovo, where did you call from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The first time that I went to Kosovo, it was during the bombing. The police headquarters did not have a constant location but moved around, depending on the situation, for security reasons. The first time I went to Pristina, the headquarters was across the road from the Bozur Hotel in the very centre of Pristina. It was on the fourth floor. I went up there. I dialled the number mentioned here. That's a Belgrade number without an extension before it for Belgrade or for Pristina. I contacted a person who told me how I should act; that I should go in the direction of Skopje. There would be a Golf car driving in front of me, it would be a dark red colour, metallic, that I should follow that car and that everything would proceed as agreed, everything would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you call from the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I got that number when I set out from Belgrade. That was my connection so that I wouldn't waste time because the matter was urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you called from the police headquarters. Why did you call from that place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: From Pristina. Well, that was the safest place. I thought it was my service, my people. Why would someone else have to listen to this conversation? And I was told I could use the telephone in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: General Zekovic, when I set out from Belgrade. And every time I set out from Belgrade I received all my instructions from General Zekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, during that time, could you normally call a Belgrade number from Kosovo without using the area code?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Only from the headquarters. From elsewhere in the town you would have to dial the area code, but in the Pristina headquarters there was always a direct line, as if you were calling to Belgrade from Belgrade. That was the case in Bujanovac. And it was a special line, a special connection, between the headquarters and the MUP, and I thought it was normal for that to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we have your statements to Mr. Stankovic and Mr. Dilparic in which you said that you spoke to Mr. Lukic, and you told us in the statement that you gave to Mr. Stankovic what he said to you on the first occasion, that is, when you took the bodies from Janjevo to Petrovo Selo. When I say "first occasion," I mean the first occasion you went to Kosovo which would be the second trip you made. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it can be -- if it just can be pointed out where in the Dilparic statement we can find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not in Mr. Dilparic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the second occasion when you went to Kosovo, did you call the number you were given?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Always the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you call it? Did you dial it on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said you spoke to Mr. Lukic. Can you tell us what he said to you on the second occasion that you went to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: When I dialled the number, I was almost sure it was Lukic's voice. Whether it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we are going to get to that. The question is: What did he say to you when you dialled the number on the second occasion that you went to Kosovo to collect bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That voice, let's say, told me that I should go in the direction of Skopje, that I would have a Golf car driving in front of me, dark red metallic in colour, and that I should follow it, which is what I did of course. In the direction of Skopje at the crossroads for Lipljani and Janjevo, I turned left towards Janjevo. The Golf stayed there and I drove on for another kilometre or a kilometre and a half and arrived in the centre of Janjevo where I was met by the local policemen. There was a Niva-make car in which they set out in front of me toward the hills. I drove the truck as far as I could, and when I could go no further, I stopped. On that occasion there was a small loader, a tractor with a scoop in front and one in back. One was wider and one was smaller, a bucket. It went to the nearby woods. I could hear the sound of the machine working. I waited about half an hour. A tractor full of soil turned up. They tipped up the trailer and this one loaded the bodies onto my truck. That was that second trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, as I said, this is in your statement already and we have time limitations, so, Mr. Protic, I'm going to ask you to please just answer the questions directly. You said that that was your second trip just now. Can you recall whether or not --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- on the occasion that you went to Janjevo, whether it was the first trip or the second trip? I ask you because in the statement that you gave to Mr. Stankovic, at page 2 in the English version, you say: "On the first occasion he ordered me to go to Janjevo and report to the local police." Was that the second or the first trip to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In connection with the bodies or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In connection with the bodies you are speaking of.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The first trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking you now is when you called the number on the second trip that you made to Kosovo in connection with collecting bodies, what did he say to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The voice on the phone told me on the second occasion that I should go to Kosovska Mitrovica, to the southern part, near the cargo railway station, and there I would be met by the people I should contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you carried those bodies that you collected there to Petrovo Selo. Who told you to take those bodies to Petrovo Selo? Or why did you take them to Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The voice -- well, I followed orders, of course. The voice on the other end of the telephone line told me that I should go to Petrovo Selo, that I should drive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the third occasion, when you said you drove --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: On the third occasion, it was the same telephone, the same voice --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did that voice --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: -- to Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could you just tell us what the person told you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That person told me to go to the parking lot behind the Rilindija building, and there were trucks there. I would be met there by some men who would tell me which truck to take. There were four or five other trucks on the parking lot and that truck, the one I was told to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who met you there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Policemen, local policemen or perhaps reserve police officers. I don't know because I hadn't seen them before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say what rank they were, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Those were police officers' insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall the ranks of these persons, the highest rank of anybody you saw there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: When? On which occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The third occasion you went to Kosovo in connection with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see any senior ranks, any high ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. On that occasion you took the bodies to the 13th May police centre in Batajnica. Why did you take the bodies there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That was what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The voice I had the telephone contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the second occasion you went to Kosovo and you went to the southern part of Kosovska Mitrovica and collected bodies, you were met at the place the bodies were by whom, by members of what organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: There were several people there. In my estimate, around 15 of them. They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they belong to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were chiefs of secretariats sent to Kosovo from Serbian municipal secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is chiefs of secretariats of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And heads of crime services of their respective centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you to a couple areas of the statements that you gave, the statement you gave on the occasion to Prosecutor Stankovic and your sworn evidence to the Belgrade court last month. I'm going to ask you a question. You said in the statement to Mr. Stankovic: "I was supposed to call a land-line" -- and that's page 2, the middle paragraph. "I was supposed to call a land-line telephone number 011-281-9074 but without dialing the area code number. In all three instances when I dialled this number, the telephone was answered by General Sreten Lukic, who was one of the assistant ministers and a commander of all police forces in Kosovo-Metohija. I knew General Sreten Lukic personally and I could recognise his voice because I was his driver for six months. I often drove him to Kosovo-Metohija and spoke with him on the phone; therefore, I can state without doubt that I could recognise his voice, which made it unnecessary for him to introduce himself because I knew who I was speaking to."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to object to this kind of leading questions to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't reached the question yet, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. This is the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not immediately obvious that it can be objected to because all that's being referred to is evidence already given by the witness. So we repel that objection. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you gave testimony to the court in Belgrade, at page 19 of the English transcript you said: "Knowing that I was at the staff and he was Chief of Staff and I drove Obrad while in the staff, we often talked on the telephone. The Belgrade number I called, I am 99 per cent and even 100 per cent sure that I contacted Lukic." And at page 27 you said to the Belgrade court again: "It is my deep conviction that says I was 99.9 per cent sure that it was the voice of General Lukic." But the first question is something about before but on this specific issue: Is the evidence you gave under oath to the Belgrade court and the statement you gave to Mr. Stankovic true or not true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were the driver of Mr. Lukic. When were you his driver? What period?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In 1990, or rather, from 1990, or rather, in the 1990s on and off because I would work for him and then have a bit of time off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When, if you can remember, was the last period in the 1990s that you were his driver?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I can't pin-point the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from driving for him, did you have any other opportunity prior to -- to the circumstances when you made these three calls from Kosovo that we just spoke of to hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was able to recognise all the voices I would hear over the telephone without the persons introducing themselves. Even now of course, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I have been or I had been working in the service since 1975, and then with the start of the 1980s as the unrest in Kosovo escalated and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So would you say that you -- well, let me just ask the question. Approximately how long - I know you can't be exact - have you known General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: For some ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we are in 2007 now. Ten years would take us back to 1999 [sic] --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: But you have to count in the five years I have been retired. I was talking about the period up to the date of retirement. It was ten years up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Before I move on from that, you say that -- or do you know how many trucks with bodies were taken to Batajnica? You have told us that you took two loads. Do you know how many loads in all were taken there from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: According to the stories of how many bodies were uncovered,

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that answer that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be attended to, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just answer this question without calling any names. How many trucks do you know -- or how many truck-loads do you know of bodies were taken to Batajnica, apart from the two you took there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The truck from Zajecar which transported some 20 bodies but then broke down. Do you want to count that one in? And then there was the refrigerator truck, or are you referring to something extra?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just how many trucks, apart from your two trips, how many deliveries of bodies do you know of to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I can tell you the persons who did the trips, but how many trips they did, I don't know. I can tell you who drove the trucks in addition to me, and then you should ask them about the number of trips made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Who drove the trucks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were in Bujanovac and a doctor from the MUP came there and spoke to you. Firstly, what were you doing in Bujanovac, were you working there or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: After my return from Kosovo, I was sent to Bujanovac, also to the staff in the so-called land zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just where is Bujanovac?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In the south of Serbia, near to Vranje near to the Macedonian border --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, could you give that answer again. You said in the south of Serbia. Could you continue from there because the interpreter did not catch what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the south of Serbia near to the Macedonian border and the Kosovo border; the closest town in Kosovo is Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said a doctor spoke to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am referring to matters that are on page 9 of this interview with Mr. Dilparic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said a doctor spoke to you. Who is this doctor, can you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Can I give you his last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Dr. Batnozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his position then when he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He holds the rank of colonel and is the chief of medical corps of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you remember when he spoke to you about retirement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: At the time, a multi-ethnic police force was supposed to be set up down there at Bujanovac composed of Albanians and Serbs. They were supposed to work as a unified force, and it was supposed to be operational. And he was down there at Bujanovac with a medical team to carry out regular medical check-ups in order to select the possible candidates for the police force. His -- he was stationed at the Bujanovac spa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. When, when did he speak to you about retirement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you remember the month in 2001 that you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I have a decision with me to that effect. I can show it to you and it bears the date of my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the month that you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: At the end of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, which month? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be allowed to look at his document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What document do you have there that you want to look at?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The decision on my retirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you give the document to the usher, please; he'll show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A copy of this document was disclosed to the Defence, and there's a translation here in English. The Prosecution are not really intending to use this document, but if he cannot remember the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems reasonable. Mr. Lukic, have you any objection to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just confirm the date of your retirement from that document, please. Tell us -- tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28th of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how long before that were you -- were you approached by this doctor, the colonel, in Bujanovac?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Since I spent the total of six months at Bujanovac when the refrigerator truck case started, that's to say the transportation of dead bodies, I followed the press and I cut out all the articles related to this issue. I would have the clips taken out and I set them aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just give me a time-period, a time-period, about how long before your retirement officially did the doctor speak to you about retirement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: One month, approximately one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you say -- well, who approached who? Did you approach him or did he approach you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He approached me, and he advised me that since I had spent a great deal of time in the -- working in the field that I should get retired and that the circumstances were propitious for that at that moment. Later on I realised that conditions for retirement at the time were, in fact, not favourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this you say was at about the time when the issue of the refrigerator truck being found was in the press? Don't nod. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did that colonel, doctor, tell you to go anywhere or do anything?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you do next, if anything, in respect to your retirement after he spoke with you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He told me, when you come down for a weekend, that I should get in touch with him, that he had the people who do -- take care of the matter and that it would only take a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And go down to where? Where was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That I should get in touch with him whenever I come to Belgrade for a weekend, that he would see to the matter, that they would expedite the procedure, and that it would all be over in a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you do anything having -- him having told you that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Since I had spent a lot of time out afield and that I had worked a great deal more than any of my other colleagues in the service, I contemplated the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you act upon it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Of course I did, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I came to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: His office in the building where his headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which city?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did he direct you to do anything from there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, he only said I should contact him and that he would do everything, and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He sent me to the health centre of the MUP in Durmitorska Street where the headquarters are -- is, and there I addressed the doctor from the commission who took me to two or three offices, and it was all over in a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you examined medically?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, if you think that a conversation amounts to a medical examination, then yes. There were no blood tests, no heart echoes or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know on what grounds you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was immediately told what my diagnosis was, yes, I can tell you if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please, go on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Allegedly I had high blood sugar, 20 units. I had arrhythmic beating of the heart, and a neuropsychiatrist said that I had night sweats and nightmares of being persecuted in closed spaces. None of this is true. Then the commission was scheduled, and I was there with the workers from Zajecar, not the workers from Belgrade. I was among the first to be called. When I entered before the commission, they immediately congratulated me and they said, You're a pensioner as from now. And that was the end of it. I wasn't with the commission from Belgrade because my colleagues from Belgrade knew me and they would have been surprised, how come I was being pensioned off when I had never even been on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, can we move on quickly, Mr. Protic. Do you recall that you were interviewed on many occasions by a team in respect to the truck with bodies that was found in the Danube in respect that investigation in the year 2001 and that team was led by Mr. Karleusa and Mr. Furdulovic do you recall that? Please speak your answer. Do you remember that you were interviewed by Mr. Karleusa and Mr. Furdulovic in 2001 in respect to the matters you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and the same Karleusa and Furdulovic later took me to Petrovo Selo to show them the spot where I had unloaded the bodies, and I did that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you present when that area in Petrovo Selo was exhumed, was dug up?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I pointed to the spot where I had unloaded that, and I was present until they found the first body. When they assured themselves that this was correct, then I was free to go and I was not present any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After the statement or the interviews conducted by Mr. Karleusa's team, you and -- that is Exhibit P586 I think the report is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will not call it up, Your Honours. I just do that for the purpose of cross-reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke with -- in the interview we spoke of earlier with Judge Dilparic. Now, in neither of those interviews is it recorded that you said that you called and spoke with Sreten Lukic when you went to Kosovo to collect bodies. I'd like you to tell the Court why is it on both of these occasions when you had the opportunity to do so, you did not mention that it was Sreten Lukic that you called when you went to Kosovo to collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I have to object to the form of the question because my learned friend is judging now in advance that this was Sreten Lukic, and we will show you that it wasn't. So rephrase the question and -- he should rephrase the question and put it in the manner the witness answered, and maybe to ask him whether it's true or not or -- and why it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That type of objection is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- we repel that objection, Mr. Stamp, and we'll allow you to ask the question. The objection is unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One also has to, if I may say so, Your Honour, be sensitive to the circumstances of some witnesses and ought to be careful in the way objections are expressed, in that -- when I say one ought to be careful in the way objections are expressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can see nothing wrong with the way in which that objection was expressed except that it was without any foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why on those previous occasions when you had the opportunity to do so did you not mention that -- the contact, that you called with Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: First of all, if I was pensioned off in two days' time and I would have had to work for another five years in normal circumstances and my wife was employed in the ministry, as were my son and daughter, I was afraid that they would be dealt with in the same way I had. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time when you gave those two statements I just referred to, what was the official position of Sreten Lukic, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the sector and he was the assistant minister of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that your wife and your son and daughter were employed by the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They still are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your interview with Judge Dilparic -- and I refer to the bottom -- the last few lines of page 13 in English -- maybe I should just correct something before I proceed with the question. It is written here in English: "When I got the summons to come to the office of The Hague Tribunal in Jevrema Grujica Street I called the Chef de Cabinet Sreten Lukic as I had done when I got the summons and I informed the MUP that I had received the summons and what to do. They took my telephone number and said they would get back to me. They never called me, and on every previous occasion before I received the summons, they would ring me and send a car for me to take me to the interview and I would get instructions what I was to say and how." Firstly it says here: "I called the chef de cabinet Sreten Lukic ..." Did you actually call Sreten Lukic or did you call the chef de cabinet of Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: All the conversations with Sreten Lukic are done through the chef de cabinet. His name was Zoran Alimpic and it was him I called on that occasion and I told him that I had received the summons for 1330 in the Palace of Justice in the war crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said on previous occasions they would ring you, send a car for you to take you to the interview, and you'd get instructions or you'd get instructions what you were to say and how. And you were asked who would call you, and you said Karleusa. What I'd like to ask you is this: What do you mean when you said that you would get instructions what you were to say and how? Can you just explain that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The chief of Karleusa always sent a driver to pick me up and take me to the centre at Makis to come and give a statement or what I knew about the events at the time. Mr. Karleusa never told me what to say. He always told me that I should only tell the truth because I had no reasons to conceal or withhold anything. So I said everything, both to Judge Dilparic and to the special court. I wasn't trying to incriminate anyone, I wasn't trying to invent charges against someone because I had a grudge or anything like that. I was simply and purely telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, we've I think reached the point where you've had as much time as you can have today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, as a matter of fact, when the witness said: "I was simply and purely telling the truth," I was just about to say that I had nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, are you the only counsel with cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
