utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Protic. My name is Branko Lukic, and I appear for General Sreten Lukic. I will have quite a few questions for you, and I ask you to concentrate and to give answers that are as precise as possible. You were asked before the court in Belgrade, as there seems to be a misunderstanding about your address in the Obalski Radnika Street?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you come by that flat or apartment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I heard that the MUP had 16 vacant flats in that location intended for the Milicionar sports club and I moved in in order to get away from Batajnica, because Batajnica holds very bad memories for me. I wanted -- or rather, I didn't want to spend the rest of my life in Batajnica or even to pass through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you entered that flat illegally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You asked Sreten Lukic to give you a flat when he was head of public security and he refused. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic offered me a vacant flat which had in it a policeman who was an invalid. He had been injured in Kosovo and he had three children. He sent me to see that flat and evict that man and move in. I would never have done that even if I had had to live in a tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But your son lives in the flat you left?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's my flat, my wife and I got 50/50 each of that flat, and my son remained in that flat with his wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you're saying what you're saying for the very reason -- and you're incriminating Sreten Lukic for the very reason that he did not give you unlawfully a second flat; he refused to break the law. You already had received a flat and you asked him to do that while he was holding the post of chief of the public security sector. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Are you reading my mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that. How did it come about that you made a statement to the Administration for Organised Crime on the 29th of June, 2006?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prosecutor Stankovic, how come you made that statement? Were you summoned?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was summoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I responded to the summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: To Makisa to the war crimes department where the Kostic Aleksandar was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went to the MUP, not to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was in the Prosecutor's office before that when I was telling the chef de cabinet Zoran Alimpic that he should tell Mr. Lukic that I was going there, that it had to do with the refrigerator truck case and that it might be a good idea for us to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes. I'm waiting for the interpretation to end. You have already told us this and you have also already told us that no one from Mr. Lukic's office wanted to give you any instructions as to how you should testify. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were questioned in 2006 in the Prosecutor Stankovic's office, was Bozo Predalic there, your counsel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He's not my counsel and he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statement signed by Prosecutor Stankovic, it says: "Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, police directorate, criminal investigation police administration." On the same document there are some initials DJ/AK. I would like to know who was acting in this case where you made the statement. Was it the police, because that's what the heading would indicate, or was it the prosecutor who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was summoned to Makisa to the criminal police administration where Kostic Aleksandar was the chief. He was there. There was also the judge you mentioned, Jankovic or Jankusic and also present was an operative who took notes on a computer. He took down what we were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the end of the document we see that DJ in fact refers to Dragan Jenic, who was the recording clerk?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, his nickname was Junice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then his name is in the wrong place. He should have been second, but according to the way these initials are ordered, it appears that he was supposed to lead the questioning?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So DJ and AK, Dragan Jenic and Aleksandar Kostic are employees of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were questions put to you by the prosecutor or by the inspector?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So both put questions to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to dwell a little on the next two paragraphs of your statement made to Prosecutor Stankovic of the 29th of June, 2006. I'm interested in the following. On the third page in English, the last paragraph, and the next one; and B/C/S version, second page, third and fourth paragraphs, you say: "On the 5th of December, 2003, I made a statement to investigating Judge Dilparic where I explained my participation in the transport of mortal remains from Tekija and Kosovo and Metohija, and now I can say that I made four trips in total and in all four trips, on all four occasions I drove dead bodies in a truck. I made the first trip during the bombing. I think it was in late April or early May 1999. The other trips were three to five days apart. I received orders for each trip from Petar Zekovic, who was at the time the head of the administration for joint affairs and assistant minister of the interior. There were always verbal orders containing instructions as to how and where I should pick up the truck, which truck it would be, and where I should go to collect the bodies." You testified about the same event in Belgrade before the judge of the district court and the investigating judge in Belgrade, Milan Dilparic, told you it was your duty to tell the truth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you were also told not to withhold anything. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same judge told you that it was a crime to give false evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told by the court in Belgrade that you are not duty-bound to answer questions if your answer would have exposed either you or your close relatives to severe disgrace, substantial material damage, or criminal prosecution. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The judge then asked you whether you had understood these warnings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said that you had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in 2003 you were telling the truth to Judge Dilparic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That you didn't know who you spoke to in Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that reference, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's English version of the statement from 2003, English page 2, paragraph 3. And the paragraphs are from -- the first paragraphs were read from the 2006 statement. It's page 3, last paragraph. But the warnings given by the judge in 2003 are on page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm now lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everybody's lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't think you'd read anything from 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 2006 I read the warnings given by the judge -- actually, I didn't read them; I go through it through questions. But you can find all the warnings on page 3, paragraph 3 -- page 2, paragraph 3, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought these -- these warnings don't come from 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why are we talking about 2006? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm questioning him now on two paragraphs from his statement in 2006, paragraphs from page 3, last paragraph, and the next paragraph on the next page. And I will go through every sentence of these paragraphs, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you go to line 53 -- sorry, page 53, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "I would now like to dwell a little on the next two paragraphs of your statement made to Prosecutor Stankovic of the 29th of June" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I now have that clear. What I'm not clear about is -- just carry on. I'll catch up eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour, that I will be able to show you what I want. But from line 10 we are on the next statement. When I said: "You testified about the same event in Belgrade before the judge," it's a reference -- it's a reference to the statement from 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the –

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the reference to not knowing who he was speaking to in Pristina is where?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in 2003, the statement to the Judge Dilparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, please. Yes, Your Honour, it's page 13, first line. "The contact, I did not know who was on the other side of the phone ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 13, line 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mine is: "Did they wear caps ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just informed that there are two translations, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you help me with where this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, give me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in my copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now it's page 8, middle of the page. Your Honour, it's on the page we quoted. If you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are the same -- these are the same conversations as the witness now says were with Mr. Lukic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, why are we not getting straight to the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Protic, you were asked some questions just now about whether you told the truth at the interview -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now. You were asked whether you gave the truth to Milan Dilparic in December 2003, and once you told him that you got a Belgrade number in Pristina, you then told him you didn't know who was at the end of the line, and you then said: "I never saw these people. I didn't have any direct contact with them, face-to-face as they say." Now, you've told us today the person you were speaking to was Mr. Lukic. So which is the truthful version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you at the outset what the circumstances surrounding my retirement were and that the rest of my family were employees of the MUP. I withheld that fact for the sake of my family. I did not want to expose them to possible risks or repercussions and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the answer you gave Mr. Lukic when he asked you. You told him that the evidence you gave to Dilparic was all true, and that includes the bit that says: "I didn't know who I was speaking to," or dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic asked me whether I had answered the questions the judge put to me and I said yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but did you tell the whole truth, which you were obliged to tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was afraid. I didn't tell the whole truth because I was afraid for my family and I was sent to retirement in a summary procedure precisely for that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the part you did not tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This precise part; namely, that I spoke to General Lukic, who was chief of sector at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were answering the judge's questions, did you know that an indictment was issued against Sreten Lukic before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: First of all, the indictment wasn't issued --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave your statement to Dilparic in 2003, in the month of December. It was actually on the 5th of December, 2003. This is the very statement we were referring to right now.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Sreten Lukic was indicted by the Tribunal two or three months before your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He was still in Belgrade, and in my view his position was still quite powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that you made such statements because you were afraid of the possible repercussions for your family, as you had been retired. The statement you gave to Karleusa was in the month of June of 2001. At the time, you did not know that you were going to be retired at all.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was already retired at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the month of June of 2001?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us just now that you were retired on the 28th of December, 2001, and you showed us the decision and you read the date out to us from that decision.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: You're right. I was still working.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not fearful of anything at all in June 2001?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I might have been. The job I was doing wasn't simple and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on. You're dealing with the 2006 statement given to Stankovic. You said that for each of the trips you were issued an order from the Assistant Minister Zekovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you say Petar Zekovic was the chief of your administration.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: For joint affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Gojko Todorovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Was it Zekovic who was chief of administration or was it Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Zekovic was chief of administration for joint affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Gojko Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Gojko Todorovic was chief of department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And not of the administration?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Every order you received from Petar Zekovic was, according to your words, verbal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was someone else present at the time Zekovic was issuing you with orders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The first time it was Nenadic Dragic who told me what I was supposed to do. He told me to report to General Zekovic. On that occasion General Zekovic and I were alone and he told me what to do; however, it was Nenadic Dragic who told me to report to him, my chief of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 3, last paragraph of that same statement, you say there that: "Every time the order contained instructions as to how and where to take a truck, which truck I should take, and where I should head to collect the bodies."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I right, therefore, that already in Belgrade you were aware of the location you were to go to and what you were supposed to transport?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, because during the bombing, the staff, or rather, the head office of the police, would frequently change their HQ. If I -- and it may have happened that even if I had it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer; it was incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, could you give the -- give us again the last part of that last answer. You told us that the police would frequently change their headquarters, and could you tell us the rest of the answer again because the interpreters did not pick it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would change the location of the headquarters due to bombing. The NATO forces were bombing Pristina. If they were at one location on a day, they might change that location twice or even thrice in a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, my question to you was not where the HQ was located; rather, you stated that every time the order contained instructions, and, among other things, you say that it contained instructions as to "where I was to go to collect the bodies." This is what you told Stankovic in 2006.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every time when you spoke to Zekovic, at that time you already knew where you were supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No. Zekovic would tell me to go to Pristina to report to a certain location, but then in the meantime the location would change and I would have to get in touch with the HQ from where they would tell me where to go next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would report to the HQ. Would you go there physically?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'd go there physically and I would there use, or rather, dial the telephone number that was mentioned here. I would dial the number and then I would receive my instructions as to where I was supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that telephone line later. Rather, tell us what that telephone number was.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Can I consult my notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can't. Do you know the number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Of course I don't. Why should I remember it? I have it in my notes and I had it on me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you orally testify before Judge Dilparic? Before our court it is not allowed for witnesses to use any documentation whilst testifying. Did you give the telephone number to Judge Dilparic and Prosecutor Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does that rule come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- if you testify orally, you cannot use your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were tell him not to use his notes here --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm also telling him not to use his notes here right now -- for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, carry on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you didn't know the number from memory before Judge Dilparic and Prosecutor Stankovic, in what way were you able to give them the number? Was it that Stankovic suggested to you what the number was? How were you able to give that telephone number in your evidence, then, if you don't remember it now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I had that telephone number down on a piece of paper and I kept it for a long time together with my driver's licence and my documents in my pocket, and when Mr. Dilparic asked me that question I took that piece of paper out and I gave it to him. I didn't know it by heart. I don't have the habit of memorising such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. What about Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Same there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further on in the statement, in the English version it's page 4, paragraph 1, and that's the same statement given to Stankovic, you state: "When I got to Kosovo and Metohija and when I was in Pristina or in Kosovska Mitrovica, I would report on a fixed number." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please give me answers that are as precise as possible. When you arrived in Kosovo and Metohija for the first time, you called from the MUP HQ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second time you also phoned from the MUP HQ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the third time, again you called from the MUP HQ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You tell us today that Zekovic told you - and this is page 30, line 20 - to call from the MUP HQ the telephone number he gave you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Zekovic know that Sreten Lukic was the head of the MUP HQ?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. They are generals. I'm just a common private, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Petar Zekovic upon your return where it was that you called the number he gave you from? And I'm referring to the first time you came back from the trip. Did you tell him, I called such and such a number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I told him that the mission was accomplished and that was it. I didn't go into who I got in touch with, so on and so forth. My task was completed and I -- and that was the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first time you came to the MUP HQ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Do you mean going to Kosovo or the refrigerator truck to Tekija?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I'm interested in Janjevo. That was the first time; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went to the HQ.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which was the telephone that you used?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The HQ was across from the street of Bozur, on the third floor. It was the premises of a company of sorts. I went upstairs and there were a couple of police officers there. It seems to me that I met a Senijevic and Mijatovic. As I was entering the building, I went upstairs. I conducted that conversation, and from there I went on further to complete the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received supplemental information from the Prosecutor, on the last page of which it is stated: "The first time he called from the furniture company Novi Dom."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Novi Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "The second time from a company in the centre of Pristina across from Hotel Bozur."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it Hotel Bozur the place where you called on the first or the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a hotel, it was a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you call? On which occasion was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I called from both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you went to Janjevo, what was the location where you phoned from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I know there was a staff here and there. Where it was exactly at that point in time, I don't know. But I used those two locations to make phone calls from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know from what place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is overlapping between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third time I went to the parking lot and there were policemen there and vehicles and trucks and all sorts of things, and everything was ready to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on the third occasion you didn't call from the headquarters, you went there directly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's right there. You could see a whole lot of vehicles and policemen from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But when I put the question to you, you said that on all three occasions you went to the headquarters and called from the headquarters, so this part of your statement is not correct.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, no, that last bit, no. But I always reported to someone. On that third occasion I saw the vehicles and I saw a whole -- a crowd of policemen. I guess that was the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on the first occasion, who permitted you to call? Who allowed you to use the phone?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to the first office as I entered, and nobody stopped me or told me not to use the phone. There was chaos there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you dialled from that phone without using the area code?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was that a Belgrade number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't using the area code, so probably it was a Belgrade number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many Belgrade numbers were there in the staff which moved on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, how would I know? You have to ask the communications people about that, the ones who maintained communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're going too quickly between question and answer at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dialing, as you say, on the second phone of the Belgrade line in the headquarters, and the headquarters changed locations several times a day due to the bombing, so you dialled a number without using the area code for Belgrade or you could have got a number in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know anything about telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you could have got any SUP in Kosovo which also had a Belgrade line?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, that's possible also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You don't recall the name of the man whose office you entered to use the telephone number you had noted down?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: There were no name tags on those offices. At that time it didn't matter who had what rank and who was sitting where or doing what, at least in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I was clumsy in putting my question. Do you remember the name of your colleague, the policeman whose office you entered and whose telephone you used?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, in the corridor I asked someone for a telephone and he said, "You can go in there." I don't know who the person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not ask specifically for a Belgrade line?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No. I just said, "I need a telephone to dial a number."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if it was a Pristina line, you could have called without using the area code and got a Pristina number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told it was a Belgrade line. Zekovic told me when I was setting out that they had a Belgrade line. Whether it was a Pristina line or a line of any other town in Kosovo, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, assuming that they let you use a telephone which had the Pristina line and not the Belgrade line, when you dialled the number you would have got a number in Pristina because you didn't use an area code?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I asked for a telephone to dial a number, a Pristina number. I dialled that number and I got what I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the same thing happen on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the third time, you didn't call?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I could already see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we received additional information, supplemental information, from the Prosecutor and it's also contained in your statement, the one of 2006 before Dragoljub Stankovic. The Prosecutor refers to page 4 and you say: "General Lukic gave instructions to the witness to go to the parking lot of Rilindija." And in the case of the Stankovic statement -- well, we established that it's not correct that at the Rilindija parking lot it was General Lukic who directed you there and that this part of your statement, wherever it is that you mention it, is not correct. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, 12 years have elapsed. There are things I remember, things I don't remember, things I remember vaguely or that come back to me. So both possibilities are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that you recalled it for the first time last year about Lukic, but let's move on. You say that the first -- on the first occasion you were told only to report to a certain place, a certain location, and that somebody else would give you further instructions. That was a brief conversation. Is that correct on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Not instructions. They said, "Drive in the direction of Skopje and there will be a vehicle driving in front of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's brief. Okay. On the second occasion when you went towards Mitrovica you say, "Report to Mitrovica to the railway station." Is that more or less what you were told?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the cargo or freight railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So again it was a brief conversation and there's no third conversation. You did not introduce yourself to Sreten Lukic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he did not introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. The fixed number that you say you called on two occasions, did you ever dial it from Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No. After loading, there was no need to call again because I knew where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, with reference to the two paragraphs we are talking about you said that you received orders from Petar Zekovic to go to Kosovo and Metohija, and when you got there in Pristina or in Kosovska Mitrovica, you reported to a fixed telephone number. So what you said before Stankovic in 2006 is not correct. You did not call from Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: It's correct, I didn't. May I go on? I didn't because I had already received instructions in Pristina. Had there been any doubts on my part, had there been any changes, then I would have called from Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you where -- whether this part where you say that you called that telephone number from Mitrovica is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, not from Pristina -- no, no, it was from Pristina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so there was no further need for me to call from Mitrovica. Had I had any doubts, I would have called from Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just again help me, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that reference in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's English version, page 4, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not my paragraph. This -- we're now on the Stankovic statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not on my paragraph 1 on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously there is a different set-up of pages, so give us one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't want to object, but I think just for the references, counsel should use the e-court page numbers. He's using the unrevised translation, I believe. The final CLSS translation, as indicated, was delivered to the Defence and is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the one that you should use, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, but we didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We just got those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We just got them. As you know, I'm really trying to be as precise as possible and to guide Your Honours and my learned friends to specific paragraphs but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to see this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Give us half a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think I have it if it's the reference to: "The next time, he told me to go to the southern part of Kosovska Mitrovica and gave me the name of a contact person."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Because I think what counsel is saying is that the witness said in the statement that he called from Kosovska Mitrovica. There are just two references to Kosovska Mitrovica in the statement, in this statement. That is the one just quoted by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second one is where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the second one is in the middle of the same page where he said: "It was Petar Zekovic who gave me orders to go to Kosovska Mitrovica. Once I arrived there in Pristina or Kosovska Mitrovica, I was supposed to call."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now clear. It then says: "In all three instances when I dialled the number, the telephone was answered by General Lukic." Now, as I understand what the witness is now saying is that there was only one occasion when he telephoned and there was an answer by General Lukic, because he said on the third occasion he phoned nobody and he's now said that in Kosovska Mitrovica he didn't phone anyone. It's important we're clear on this, Mr. Stamp. That's what he now seems to be saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would beg to differ with respect. He could be asked again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask him. Mr. Protic, there were three occasions when you collected bodies in Kosovo -- in Kosovo, you say. On the first occasion you've told us that you did phone a number and spoke to a person you say was General Lukic. The second time I think the journey was to Kosovska Mitrovica. Did you on that occasion telephone and speak to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Pristina I went to Kosovska Mitrovica. In Pristina I was told where to report in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On that occasion did you speak to General Lukic or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be certain I spoke to General Lukic. I'm 90 or 99 per cent certain, but it was always the same voice that gave me instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to be more precise than that, I'm afraid. You've just been telling us that you had no reason to make a phone call on that trip. Now, are you saying that in Pristina you made a phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked whether I phoned from Mitrovica. I did not phone from Mitrovica, but I phoned from Pristina and then I went to Mitrovica. And after that, I didn't have any other conversations. I set out towards Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you phoned from Pristina, who was it you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same telephone number and the same voice as on the first occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be a hundred per cent sure it's Lukic, but in my opinion - and I still hold that opinion today - it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, that would appear to cover two occasions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, do you know Milan Cankovic, a communications person from MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you last see him or hear from him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Just before my retirement. I used to see him down there at Bujanovac when we were in the field. That was before my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your statement dated the 5th of December, 2003, in the English version on page 5, paragraph 2, you say: "I went to Pristina. I was given a Belgrade number that I was supposed to call from Pristina. A man answered the phone. He set out in front of me in the direction of Skopje, and some 20 kilometres from Pristina in the direction of Skopje a dark blue Golf turned off to the village of Janjevo. I followed the vehicle. As we reached the village of Janjevo, the car in front of me pulled up beside the road and the local police took over from there." Here you say that you were given a Belgrade number, that a man answered, who set out in a dark blue Golf vehicle in front of you. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: First of all, your question was wrongly put. I dialled the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... In front I gave different -- again different setup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question and then we'll go back to the difficulties we have with the pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I dialled the number. A man answered the phone who told me, "A Golf vehicle will be riding in front of you." It's not that the person who answered my phone call was riding in front of me. The person told me, "You will be heading in the direction of Skopje and there will be a Golf vehicle escorting you and it will be riding in front of you." That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, I'm reading out what your words were.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said what it is written here: "A man answered and said that he was setting out in front of me."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Can you even make any sense out of these words?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And rode in the direction of Skopije."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The formulation is wrong. One and the same person can't answer the phone and be riding in front of me. We didn't have mobile phones at the time, if this is what you have in mind. A man answered my call and gave me instructions as to what was to be done next. He told me, "You should head in the direction of Skopje and there will be a Golf in front of you." This is what I said and now what you're reading out, perhaps it wasn't written well or translated well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that at the time there were no mobile phones?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I didn't have one and I didn't know anyone who had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that on your way to Kosovo you did not speak to Vlastimir Djordjevic, a general, over a mobile phone and that he gave you instructions and directions as to where you should go?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, could you find a suitable place to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a good place enough for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the afternoon, we'll expect you to be able to identify passages accurately on the e-court copy, so somebody should work on that for you so that we can relate them, because it's very difficult to follow, otherwise, and you will lose time as a result of it, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, we now need to interrupt again for lunchtime. Would you go with the usher. You'll be away for an hour and we'll see you at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Protic. Your cross-examination by Mr. Lukic will now continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Protic, I showed you a part of your earlier statement today which you said made no logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Defence Exhibit 6D196 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive this document from Prosecution. This is a record which was made at the official premises of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia on the 27th of August, 2002. We see that the recording clerk was Aleksandar Kostic, and you were heard by members of the operative team. Let us Look at page 2 of the document which is only an excerpt of your -- of the statement. In this statement you say: "The liaison person in Pristina whose name I don't know, but it's always the same man, drove a burgundy Golf and followed me up to the intersection to Janjevo village. And after that there was another reservist whose name I don't know either, a Lada Niva was also driven in the direction of Janjevo village." Does this statement of yours also seem illogical, is this the way you put it, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the physical liaison or link, and they were driving in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also state here that it's always one and the same person. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was referring to the person in the car. I remembered the vehicle because I didn't see the person. The person was driving some 15 to 20 metres ahead of me depending on the traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said this was a liaison person?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes. A liaison, or rather, I'm -- what I meant by saying a liaison or a link was that this person and vehicle were escorting us or escorting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the only liaison person you mention in the statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this person a civilian or a police officer?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: A civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to Prosecutor Stankovic, page 3, paragraph 3, of the English version, there you state: "I made one trip to Petrovo Selo." And there you say: "Sreten Lukic issued the order to take the truck to the village of Janjevo, where I would be met by a local policeman." Was there a police officer waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a Lada Niva, who took me to the site where I was supposed, to go but all of this happened after the Golf event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you had your escort in Belgrade as well?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that answer, please, Mr. Protic. The interpreters again did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question to you was: Did you have your escort on your way from Belgrade as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, all the way through to the store where Lada Niva was waiting for me. My escort from Belgrade stopped there in front of the store and waited for me to head back. And then the police officer in Lada Niva escorted me uphill all the way up to the point where he was able to drive. And there I was met by a tractor with a trailer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had escorts consisting of Golf and your escorts from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I had my escort from Belgrade, and as for the Golf vehicle, that vehicle was leading the way, whereas my escort followed behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this is something you never told either to the investigating judge or to the working group that examined you on the 4th of June, 12th of June, and the 19th of June, 2001, as well as on the 27th of August, 2002?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the burgundy Golf car and the escort following me in all my statements, and I gave the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you never mentioned talking to Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In none of the statements I referred to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the supplemental information we received from the Prosecutor last night, there is mention of the parking lot at the Rilindija.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that a policeman waited for you there. This person who was waiting for you at Rilindija, was he a police officer or a civilian? In your evidence today you said that he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a policeman. He was wearing a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about that civilian in the Golf, where was he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That was in Janjevo. That was my liaison between Pristina and Janjevo. This has nothing to do with this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on this occasion that person wasn't present?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the person even while we were travelling to Janjevo. Even if you were to show him to me now, I wouldn't recognise him. I never saw his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us today - and I can see this in your statement as well as in today's transcript page 78, 12, or rather, page 78, lines 12 through 16, that the civilian in the Golf vehicle was present on all three occasions. What is the truth? Was he present on all three occasions or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I never saw the person. I saw the Golf vehicle only on my way to Janjevo and never again. I went to Mitrovica on my own. From Vinje [phoen] I came to the parking lot and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this isn't true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, no, it isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the liaison person was the civilian in Golf on all three occasions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: The liaison person -- or rather, the liaison was through the telephone number. That civilian in the Golf vehicle was there for the first time and he was there to take me to Janjevo. I didn't see him again, and even if you were to show him to me now I wouldn't know the man. The liaison person or the contact person was the same on all three occasions, and that was the person that I got in touch with over the phone; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This isn't what you said. I just read it out from our document 6169 where you say the contact person or the liaison person in Pristina whose name I do not know and I don't know his face, he drove the burgundy Golf vehicle. Is that part of your statement true or not true, just tell me.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. On the page 81, line 20, it says "contact person." That should be "contact person in Pristina is always the same."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we still have this document on the screen, is this your signature that we can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session for a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While there's a pause, could I inquire of whether or not the Defence is in possession of the remainder of 6D196, just so we could see the context in which this passage which was put to the witness was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it the document is available in its original language in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you will be able to deal with a translation of that, I would have thought, in your own office, Mr. Stamp, as long as you get the version in one language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, may I inquire through the Court if we could have the document, a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can provide a hard copy at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you do that just now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so that Mr. Stamp has time to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will help us with that, and if I may continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Protic, did you tell the court in Belgrade that Obrad Stevanovic in 1999 was the commander of all the PJP units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At that time I was his driver; he was the commander in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the English version of the statement made before Prosecutor Stankovic, page 2, paragraph 3, you said that one of the assistant ministers and the commander of all the police units in Kosovo and Metohija was General Sreten Lukic. Does that mean that the PJP had two commanders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I said that Sreten Lukic was the chief of the sector. Perhaps he understood it as meaning commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Sreten Lukic was the chief of the sector after these events in Kosovo, is that correct, not in 1999? Tell us if you know; if not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go to page 2, paragraph 3 of your statement before Prosecutor Stankovic, which I would like to analyse. You say that Sreten Lukic was personally known to you, that you recognised his voice because you say you had been his driver for at least six months. And you spoke to him frequently on the phone in that period. In the supplemental information we received from the Prosecution, it says that you were Sreten Lukic's driver from April to June 1999 [as interpreted]. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about these dates, or rather, this period?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I have the official document with me, I can show it to you, sending me to Kosovo. It was signed by Radmilo Bogdanovic, who was then the secretary in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, page 84, line 17, it says "1999" and should be "1990," 9-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic, the documents also show that Sreten Lukic went to Kosovo in October 1990 and that in the period you mentioned the chief of the staff in Kosovo was Obrad Stevanovic. Is it possible that you made a switch and that you were, in fact, Obrad Stevanovic's driver?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was Obrad Stevanovic's driver, that's correct. But Mr. Lukic was there for almost as long as Obrad Stevanovic was. He would come to the staff for consultations, meetings, he would be three or four times in a week. He would come and see Obrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But are you now saying that you were a driver for both of them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Correct. When Sreten Lukic arrived in Pristina, I would drive him wherever he needed to go, even to Gnjilane. On one occasion -- well, I won't go into that now. We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know your colleague Nenad Dodic, also a driver?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he Sreten Lukic's driver?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he drove him around as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct when Sreten Lukic replaced Obrad Stevanovic, his driver, Nenad Dodic, came with him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1990 to 1999, according to you, you never drove Sreten Lukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Not if you look at the documents, but when he came to Kosovo to visit while Obrad Stevanovic was there and I was the driver of the staff, I did drive him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you after 1990, between 1990 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: When Obrad Stevanovic was Chief of Staff in Kosovo, Sreten Lukic would come to visit; and whenever he did, I was his driver for visits out in the field. However, if you look at the documents, I was never appointed his personal driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall until when you were Obrad Stevanovic's driver?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Will you let me look at the official documents and I will be able to tell you the exact date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Take a look.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: From the 23rd of April, 1990, to the 31st of July, 1990. I was sent to the Kosovo SUP to be the staff driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that date, did you drive Sreten Lukic anywhere?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, no, because on the 31st of July when this ended I returned to Belgrade, and Sreten Lukic replaced Obrad Stevanovic and he took his driver, Nebojsa Dodic, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Might I tell you in the period from the 23rd of April to the 31st of July where I drove Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Thank you. You also say that you spoke on the phone to Sreten Lukic while you were his driver in the staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: While I was in the staff, close to the telephone or near the commander's office, if Sreten Lukic went somewhere outside Pristina he would call on the phone and I would answer and I would recognise his voice. It didn't happen all that often but it did happen occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you spoke to him on the phone, that means you weren't driving him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Also after 1990 when that tour expired you didn't talk to Sreten Lukic on the phone anymore?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no need either for me to call him or for him to call me. It was only when we were out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session for one moment again, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the following. Let's go back once more to 1990. How many telephone conversations were there between April and July 1990 between you and Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about something that happened 15 years ago. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to Goran Radosavljevic who turned up in Petrovo Selo, you say he was there with his small daughter and that this was some seven days before the end of the bombing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: He was there with his daughter in a camp caravan across from the main gate leading to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And does this time that you mentioned correspond with the events?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, let's say it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know at that time there was training going on in Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, there was no training going on. There were a few policemen there and the kitchen staff. There was no training going on at the time because there were air-strikes. It would have been crazy to collect policemen in one place and expose them to danger. That's my opinion and that's how it was, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there in order for you to be able to make such an assessment as this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: As I arrived there and went around the place where this was supposed to be unloaded, I went back, I had lunch and returned the truck. It could have been two, two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we have to go to the private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The decision on your retirement was signed by Sreten Lukic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably at the time as the chief of the public security sector he would have signed at least a dozen [as interpreted] such decisions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be "10.000" instead of "a dozen such decisions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did anyone force you to get retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to me by Dr. Batnozic who told me that the conditions were favourable for that at the time. What he didn't explain to me was that I was going to get the base pension rate only and that was because I had spent too little time in service and was only able to get the minimum pension. He suggested that I retire because he said, well, I had been working out in the field for a long time and I should rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You collected the relevant documents and you submitted them to the commission?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I was never on sick leave. I didn't even have a medical file. I don't even have a medical insurance card today, because I feel quite well. What sort of medical documentation was I able to submit where I don't even -- where I never went on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you had to submit some documentation. Didn't you make blood tests and other medical check-ups?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at the time I was making these medical tests there was a vacancy made for members of the gendarmerie so that the medical office was full of people at the time. However, I don't have blood sugar, I don't have arrhythmic beating of the heart. I don't have any of the neuropsychological problems that were listed there, and on the basis of that, you can judge whether I am healthy or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you hurt by the fact that you were retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Of course I was. I am being treated as -- as a person who is not fully sane, doesn't have legal capacity to the full, and my pension is far lower compared to my colleagues of my generation who continued working until 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were distressed even further by the level of your pension, by the amount of your pension?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Of course, as well as the fact that my housing problem wasn't solved. I offered Mr. Lukic to take my Batajnica apartment and to give it to an employee who had no connections with Batajnica, and I asked for an apartment in exchange for that. I didn't ask for an apartment -- an extra apartment. I wanted my apartment to be exchanged. But as a pensioner, I even am not entitled to getting any benefits in the process of buying of apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you're asking for a second apartment. You're not asking to -- to get your flat back?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I received 33 square metres of apartment from MUP, and I had 20 years of service in MUP and this was owned by my wife and myself 50/50 per cent each. My son, who is an employee of the MUP, obtained an apartment that was paid for in full by ourselves. As a MUP employee, he is never going to lodge a request to be given an apartment from MUP. That's the whole story. On one other occasion when --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please pause there. We have to move on. We have time concerns.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Very well, although what I had to say was quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecutor will be of that opinion, he will pursue these matters. I wanted to ask you something related to your health, in particular your psychological health. We received from the -- from the Trial Chamber the following statement. "This Trial Chamber is ordering you to appear between the 19th and the 23rd of February, 2007, or on another date that will possibly be notified to you to appear before this Trial Chamber in order to testify in the case "Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al." One day later, on the 5th of February, 2007, you should, by that date at the latest, send us medical documentation from the respective medical specialist who will prove that you are suffering from a psychological disorder which prevents you from testifying. Did you claim before this Trial Chamber that you were mentally unfit to testify or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the question to me again. I was focused on what you were telling me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notify this Trial Chamber - we don't know how --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: - that because of your psychological state, you are unable to testify?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I told the interpreter, or rather, the interlocutor that I do not wish to give any evidence before this Tribunal because I do not want to remind myself of these events. I was told that I had to come. In response, I said that I could obtain the neuropsychiatric findings and the not appear before the Tribunal at all. The interlocutor asked me, "How come?" Answer: "Well, I could go out into the street in my pyjamas, the police could take me to the medical centre," but at the end of the day this wouldn't work out really because any medical examination would show that I am of sound mind and I would end up before this Tribunal anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that during the war you drove doctors?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The English version of this statement, page 2, the last paragraph, and I mean the statement dated the 5th of December, 2003. For how long did this go on?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: At the time there was lady minister Leposav Kamelicevic [phoen] and Petar Zelenovic agreed through the MUP that it would be desirable for some police officers to get involved in the transportation of medical doctors treating the troops in Kosovo. I was asked to do that and I did that. The first two trips I did in my uniform, and this was the Belgrade-Pristina-Gnjilane-Pec route that I travelled on two occasions three days apart. Later on, or rather, 15 days later I drove seven to eight medical doctors of different specialisation and took back others. This was some ten days before the end of the NATO bombing and before the arrival of the NATO ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which period of time that was?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, I've just said that it was some 15 days later during NATO bombing and just before the arrival of the NATO land forces. I continued doing that later on. There was a committee set up attached to the federal government, and I remained working for the health minister with minister -- or rather, assistant minister Tomovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say: "Just before the NATO forces entered." Did you do this on a daily basis then?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Every third day or every other day I went there and back all the time because the shifts took place in 15-day cycles. After that I remained for another year and seven months after the police and army had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. Thank you. In the statement you gave to Judge Dilparic, English version page 6, top of the page, you were asked about the corpses you were transporting. The judge asked you what kind of bodies these were, were they dressed in uniforms? And you said: "There were some in uniform, some were naked, there were children, elderly, all sorts were there." In which tour did you see corpses in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: In the refrigerator truck that emerged from the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many people were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, it was unpleasant to look at them. About ten. I just took a quick look because they were already decomposing and there was a strong stench; it was highly unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with Petrovo Selo, did you put all the bodies in a single pit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Janjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before Judge Dilparic you said: "When all this finished I couldn't be there in Belgrade but I asked to go out in the field somewhere, and I was in Bujanovac, Brezova, Nevidza for six months." Did you go to the land zone of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: Well, when the newspapers started writing about it and when this refrigerator truck was reported about for the first time in the media, the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, just tell us, please: Did you ask to go? Did you go of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: I will tell you very briefly. I went to see General Lukic. General Djordjevic also arrived. He said -- he saw that I was upset and he said, "It wouldn't be a bad idea if you go to Bujanovac to be the late Dragan Bozovic's driver." He's late now. "There's not a lot of work there. You can rest and collect yourself there, and I went." I had been absent for almost two years from the place I had worked in previously, so I wouldn't have fitted in anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what you said before Judge Dilparic, that you asked to go down there, is not correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR PROTIC
utterances.text: No, I went to see General Lukic to ask for his advice, to ask him what I should do, and he suggested I should go to Bujanovac, which I agreed to do. And I can tell you that -- well, I didn't exactly have a rest, but I did manage to put some things out of my mind, to forget about some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this would conclude our cross-examination, but because of the really late disclosure of some details in connection with this witness's testimony we wish to retain the right to re-call this witness, if need be, once we have carried out our own investigation. So we ask for the possibility of examining him again, and we would also ask, not in connection with this witness, that the OTP answer a question we have, and that is (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need go no further on that point because it's not your place in this open forum to be asking questions of the Prosecution. The very fact that you've asked that question is entirely inappropriate, Mr. Lukic. This could have been dealt with in a quite different way. It's an issue; that's fair enough.
